items.heading: PRESIDENTIAL PARS
items.summary: President's notes on the death of Fred McKay, the walkers' R.W.A. 10 miles team win, the National cross-country, the delayed club photograph at Belgrave Hall and the coming track season.
items.text:
PRESIDENTIAL PARS

It is with sorrow that we advise the death of F.E. "Fred" McKay - brother of J.R. McKay, Past President, who himself died only a few months ago. Both brothers joined the Club in May 1922 and maintained a close interest in all Club happenings throughout the greater part of their lives. Our condolences are extended to Mrs. F.E. McKay.

We congratulate most sincerely our walkers on retaining the R.W.A. 10 miles championship at Redditch. This was a great victory for sound team support in a large and representative field. It was particularly pleasing to see ALAN CALLOW, our new member from the Isle of Man figuring in our winning team.

Our Cross-country runners met with extreme disappointment in the National championships at Norwich. It certainly was not our day, the redeeming feature perhaps was yet another good run by that model of consistency, GERRY NORTH, who just failed to make the international team on a bitterly cold day.

Our plan for a Club photograph was beset by adverse circumstance but nevertheless a large number of members, covering all ages and a true cross section of the club, did face RON LINSTEAD and his camera on March 13th, and we trust we shall have a valuable record of faces for posterity.

This Club photograph was originally intended for the last Saturday in January when runners, walkers would be present in good numbers at our headquarters. However it was found that the Belgravian could not appear in sufficient time to advise all members of the intended photograph and it was decided to defer it until March 13th which seemed to be the only possible alternative date. Plans were duly made, special invitations extended to Past Presidents and many others; and then the postal strike intervened and our "Belgravians" and invitations to participate could not be sent out as well in advance as we would have hoped.

However, come the day and we were very pleasantly pleased with the numbers at Belgrave Hall. One wondered how many clubs could show such a muster, and with the circumstances adverse at that.

We'll try again sometime! Meanwhile apologies to those whose invitations reached them after the event - we should have enjoyed their company.

Our oldest members present were V.P. Ernest Neville (88 years) Charlie Speechley (83) and 1932 Olympic champion Tommy GREEN (77) - the youngest were still in single figures! Harry CHURCHER winner of seven A.A.A. titles, looked as though he could do it all over again and in support were a miscellany if internationals, former and present club champions, past presidents, and good honest worthy Belgrave Harriers covering a very wide span of years.

The track and field season proper is now upon us, and we trust we shall have an enjoyable Summer season. A few trophies here and there will remind us of our full potential, and we hope we shall distinguish ourselves in Southern League, and other events.

The prime consideration on which so much depends is, of course, complete support in every possible way of our officers and the arrangements they make on our behalf. A full attendance every time will do much to take us to the top and keep us there.

items.heading: OBITUARY
items.summary: Obituaries of J.G. (Jimmy) Flatt, Blackstaffe Shield winner and member since 1921, and Vice-President W. (Bill) Redgrave, a member for over fifty years.
items.text:
OBITUARY

J.G. (JIMMY) FLATT

We have to advise the death of our old friend, Jimmy Flatt; and extend our sincere sympathy to his daughter.

Jimmy joined the Club in October, 1921, and his quiet, modest, unassuming manner quickly endeared him to our clubmates of 50 years ago.

In 1922, Jimmy was second in the Club 7-miles cross-country championship, but went one better the following year, when he won the "Blackstaffe" Shield. Second to him on that occasion was Micky Pyer, and third Bert Footer. In 1924, he took third medal in this championship.

He figured regularly in our teams during this rather undistinguished span of years, and led our scoring team home in the National cross-country championship at Beaconsfield in 1923. Jimmy's position was 91st, and our six scored 913 points, giving us 23rd place. Incidentally, this appears to have been the first occasion that we finished a team in this championship, which we were to win emphatically some years later in our history.

In Surrey County cross-country championships, Jimmy was a member of our winning team in 1926, and of our placed teams in 1923 and 1924.

His running career was interrupted by some spells of ill-health, but his affection for the Club was unimpaired, and he was truly one of those who laid foundations for those who followed.

In many years past, he had paid us the occasional visit at Wimbledon, and we were always glad to see the modest little man who had helped so much in the building up of our cross-country traditions, and retained his loyalty to the Club over so many years.

R.I.P.

W. (BILL) REDGRAVE

We have to record with regret the death of Bill Redgrave, a Vice-President of the Club, and a member for over fifty years. Bill was born and lived all his life in Westminster, and even after his retirement from the Army and Navy Stores continued to serve as an agent of our Football Scheme until a few weeks ago.

Bill helped the Club in many ways during his long membership, and many will remember his unfailing appearance at our Meetings to take charge of the programme sales in the days when a printed programme was considered a necessity.

Our sympathy is extended to his son Charlie, who figured in our walking teams at one time, and to Bill's daughter and her husband, Mr. and Mrs. S.L. King. Syd is, of course, a Life Member, and a former Hon. Treasurer and Walking Hon. Secretary.

- A.A.H.

items.heading: FROM 'The Belgravian' 25 years ago ..... and 40 years ago
items.summary: Reprinted extracts from June 1946 (the club's dominant first post-war cross-country season, including the English National team title) and March 1931 (Arthur Allum's Southern, National and International runs and the walkers' eight successive road wins).
items.text:
FROM 'The Belgravian'
25 years ago .....

JUNE 1946 ------
The first post-war Winter season was a memorable one for the Belgrave Harriers. Our cross-country runners won every open championship. In November we had the first two teams home in the South of the Thames "Junior", and the first three individuals. This in itself was a remarkable feat as all of our pre-war "cracks" cannot run in this race owing to the barring clauses. In the New Year we won the Surrey County Title, whilst our Middlesex members, running for Cadogan A.C., took the Middlesex title. This was not regarded as very extraordinary as it had been done on various occasions before the war. The South of the Thames "Senior" Race resulted in another win for us. Here again, a large number of our best men are barred. The Southern Counties Cross-Country Championship, 7½ miles instead of the usual 10, was held from Belgrave Hall. Our Captain, Tom Carter, gained a well earned and popular victory. With David Main third and four others in the first 20 positions, we gained a 99 points margin over the second team. In fact, our team of 12 was home before any other team had finished its six scoring men! Then to the much awaited English Championship of which we were the proud holders. On March 9th our lads travelled to Leamington Spa and had another battle royal with our famous Midland rivals, Birchfield Harriers. Our team finished in the first 24 positions, and after a breath-taking adding up of the scores we were acclaimed winners with a ten-points margin. We are indeed truly the Champion Club.

Of individuals, Tom Carter deserves our thanks and praise for the successful training and nursing of his team, also of course for his own brilliant running. It was a cause for general regret that Tom did not get another International vest. Len Herbert, by finishing seventh, was awarded an England vest and we congratulate Len on adding his name to the distinguished company of Belgravians so honoured in the past. It is of interest to recall them: A. Allum, H.E.Footer (3), A.W.Penny (3), C.T.Carter, J.Ginty and E.S.Stimpson. Pat Parker qualified for an England vest but chose to run for Ireland. David Main has also entered the ranks of the Internationals as he also ran for Ireland.

..... and 40 years ago

MARCH 1931 ------
Arthur Allum merits the congratulations of all upon his splendid running in the Southern Cross-country Championship. He is the first Belgrave man to finish in the first three of this race, and it should not be long befores he improves, even upon this.

Since writing the above Arthur has very nearly exhausted our supply of superlatives by finishing fifth in the National Championship, and so earned a place in the English team. The Club's best wishes go with Arthur to Ireland.

In the International Championship decided at Baldoyle Racecourse, Dublin, Arthur Allum finished ninth in the actual race and was the sixth Englishman to score. Thus England scored a very easy win and we are proud to have supplied one of the victorious team.

WITH THE WALKERS:
Our scratch teams have continued in the victorious vein and have brought the number of successive wins to eight - without doubt a unique feat in the history of road walking. The successes are as follows:-
R.W.A.'7', Enfield '7', Highgate '7', Belgrave '7', S.W.C. Godstone & Back, Cambridge '7', L.C.C. Tramways '7', Ashcombe '10'.
Len Fletcher and Frank Elson have assisted the Club in seven of these eight wins; Tommy Green six times; Fred Rickards on three occasions; Harold King, Frank Thorn and Ted Saunders each twice; and Joe King and Jack Field once each.

CROSS-COUNTRY

SECOND PLACE IN SURREY CROSS-COUNTRY - Wimbledon, January 2, 1971

Even with a great breakthrough by Guy Monnet, who finished a magnificent 14th in 41m. 57s., we were still kept out of first place in the Surrey Cross-Country Championship, over 7-miles of fog-bound Wimbledon Common.

Gerry North finished in sixth place in 40m. 12s., just under a minute behind the winner, Bob Holt of Hercules Wimbledon. Trevor Hart was just one place in front of Guy, who was followed by John Thresher, 18th, and a back-to-form Alan Black, 20th, with Tony Fairclough making up the scoring six. INTER-COUNTIES Leicester, January 16, 1971

Gerry helps Surrey to title

Lancashire went to Leicester as hot favourites for the inter-counties' title, but as at Leicester four years ago, it was Surrey that ran away with the race - and helping them was our own Gerry North.

Once again, Gerry showed his capacity to rise to the occasion, covering the near 7½-miles course in 35m. 42s., against 35m. 04s. by the winner, Trevor Wright, of Hallamshire and Yorkshire.

Lionel Mann produced a sound run, as usual, to finish 84th in 37m. 06s. for Bedfordshire and Huntingdonshire. But ahead of him was our rapidly improving R.A.F. runner, Tony Brien, who carried Wiltshire colours to 67th place in 36m. 48s. Turning his attention to the mud, also, was our road running member Brian Joines, who finished 287th in 42m. 55s. for Oxfordshire.

Apart from winning the Senior race, Surrey took third place in the Youths' event. Three Belgrave runners finished in the Country's scoring four - Bill Curtin coming home tenth in 18m. 58s. - some 32s. behind the winner- while Peter Carton was one place further back in 18m. 59s., and Tony Binda was the third Surrey man, with 26th place in 19m. 32s. John Stow also won his County colours, but was going through a rough patch when this race came round, and finished 99th in 21m. 11s., nothing like the performance we know he can produce.

items.heading: A SOUTHERN SILVER!
items.summary: Report and results of the Southern cross-country championship at Parliament Hill, where Belgrave took team second behind Reading and Gerry North finished fourth.
items.text:
A SOUTHERN SILVER !

BELS HIT FORM AT PARLIAMENT HILL

Having slipped out of a place in the Southern Cross-Country in 1970 for the first time in several years, the Bels bounced back into form in the Parliament Hill mud this February, with a highly encouraging second place.

Reading romped away with the title - helped by our old friend Dick Piotrowski in 37th place. Their total of 137 points went quite unchallenged. Our second place was a nail-biting business, however. With 221 points we had a margin of only 4 points to spare over the up-and-coming Hillingdon side, and only 5 to spare over Brighton & Hove.

It was pleasing to be the first Surrey side - ahead of the titleholders, Hercules Wimbledon - and also to take the Oddling Smee Cup, as the first Surrey club to close in a full team of 12 men.

The most heartwarming sight of the afternoon for Belgrave supporters was that of the flying figure of Gerry North, who made a thrilling attempt to recapture his title - and had he not been hit by his old enemy, the stitch, might well have done so. As it was, his fourth place in 46m. 55s. gave us a magnificent start, and with another three men in the first 34, and John Thresher in 42nd, it was a good day for the Bels. John Bicourt made a good recovery from his disappointing show in the Surrey, to finish 34th in 48m. 55s. Lionel Mann was two places ahead of John, with 32nd in 48m. 53s., but both these stalwarts were outpaced by that rising star Tony Brien - 30th in 48m. 48s. A below par Tony Fairclough made up the scoring six - in 79th place.

Pat O'Connor's 82nd place was closer to his real ability than some of his other performances lately, while it was good to see Bill Dance down from Yorkshire to carry the Belgrave colours again. Trevor Hart must have been disappointed with 123rd, but not as disappointed as Guy Monnet - the most sharply improved runner in the club - who could have expected to finish at least 100 places higher than his 151st.

A different Guy might have been seen, however, had it not been for a poisoned tooth. John Kelly was rewarded for his recent improvement with a first run in the Southern.

items.summary: Report and results of the National Cross-Country Championships at Norwich, where Belgrave finished twelfth, their worst placing for years, with Gerry North the only man in the first hundred in 18th.
items.text:
National Cross-Country Championships

Oh dear, what a calamity!
at the Royal Norfolk Agricultural Showground, Norwich, March 6, 1971

Hopes raised at the Southern took a sharp plunge at Norwich. Twelfth place was our worst in the National for a good few years. But that's the way it goes. Lose a few seconds in the National and you lose a lot of places.

We still have the men to get a high placing next year - six men in a hundred is a fair target to aim at. And it only wants a bit of application - not 200 miles a week.

This year we only managed one in a hundred - Gerry North battling magnificently against a bad cold - and ignoring his doctor's advice to give the race a miss - to finish 18th. Otherwise, our lads were solidy below par. And with only eight finishers, we didn't even challenge for the Charles Otway Cup - awarded to the first team (nine to score) outside the first three in the Championship.

items.summary: Review of Belgrave's 1971 road relay season (Thames Valley, Southern, Brighton Seafront and Hornsey relays) with team results from Cranford (fifth), the Brighton Front Relay and the Hornsey A.C. Relay (third and sixth).
items.text:
ROAD RELAYS

It cannot be said that 1971 was a vintage year for Belgrave in the road relay field. But the bright aspects are the emergence of our junior stars as forces in the senior ranks, and the continuing enthusiasm to be found in our ranks. Setbacks are inevitable from time to time, but they can also be the springboard for greater things.

It seemed that the disappointment of the National cross-country performance was still hanging over us when he went to Cranford for the annual Thames Valley relay, and fifth was the best we could manage. Colin Pearson's 13th place for the"B" team on the first leg was enough to win him his place in the team for ths following week's Southern relay, and there were promising runs from Alan Black and Chris Steer, but otherwise little of note.

Setting aside the two championships, however, from this point our form seemed to be improving.

Fresh,if that is the word, from seventh in the Southern race , we went to Brighton on April 3 for the Seafront race, and this time we managed fourth place. John Stow showed that he was recovering the form that makes him one of our brightest junior stars, with a good clocking on the first stage for the "A" team, and it was nice to see Derek Crooks turning out for us again.

Then, at Hornsey the following week, it was up to fourth place, with our junior runners again making their presence felt, and another good run from Chris Steer. Gerry North, unfortunately, was by this time feeling the full effects of his recent illness - which had possibly cost him his place in the international cross country team.

Road relay trial - Hayes, Kent - April 24, 1971

With a week to go our National Road Relay team was far from picking itself, and we were grateful to Blackheath for putting on a special trial at their Hayes headquarters.

Blackheath and Hercules-Wimbledon each fielded one team of four, and we put out three. The course was a slightly longer version of the one used for the annual open Blackheath relay in September, and measured just over three miles.

Our "A" team led on each lap, with our "B" team second on each, while our "C" finished fifth. Trials sometimes do something to sort out selection problems, but on this occasion the most important performance was put up by Guy Monnet, whose 15m. 06s. - slightly faster than the times returned by Tony Fairclough and Tony Binda - must have caused some headaches. Guy had not been seen in our teams for several weeks, and must have come within an ace of forcing his way into the National Relay team.

items.heading: National Relay
items.summary: Stage-by-stage report and full team results of the National Road Relay at Sutton Coldfield, won by Birchfield, with Belgrave 14th.
items.text:
National Relay

BIRCHFIELD BACK - National Road Relay, Sutton Coldfield, May 1, 1971

If it was like old times to see old pals of the Brighton Road, Thames Valley, win the Southern Road Relay, it was doubly like old times to see our London-to-Brighton rivals of the nineteen-thirties, Birchfield, taking the National Relay title.

But it was bad times for the Bels. With our Birmingham friends first in 4hrs. 10m. 58s., we were 4hrs. 21m. 00s. But just to show how fortunes fluctuate in this type of running, Southern winners Thames Valley were only 56s. ahead of us, in 12th place.

On the same lines as the Southern event, the race consisted of a 5.6 miles leg and a 3.1 miles leg, covered alternately, to make a total distance over 52 miles.

Hillingdon led at the end of the first lap, of 5.6 miles, and Coventry at the end of the each of the next 7 laps, except the fifth lap, when Tipton briefly took up the pace-making. Birchfield ended each of the last four laps at the front, but only after a great battle with the reigning champions, Godiva.

Laurie O'Hara got us off to a promising start. Though only 14th, his 27m. 11s. was a good time for the distance, and kept us well in touch with the leaders. Only Trevor Hart of our men could get within half-a-minute of his clocking.

At the end of the second stage, the outlook still looked promising. John Bicourt went round the shorter leg in a useful 15m. 23s., and gave us our best position of the day - eleventh.

Bill Kerr was not at his best, however, on the third leg, falling to 16th, with a time of 27m. 58s. Peter Carton, just turned 18, came into the team, and gave a hint of things to come, returning 15m. 43s. to pick up one place.

Pat O'Connor was a shadow of his real self on the next stage, dropping to 18th, with 28m. 27s. Gerry North was still fighting off the effects of his earlier illness, and took a short stage, rather than his customary long. He ran well in the circumstances, however, to cover his lap in 15m. 09s., and pull back two places.

Next, it was Lionel Mann's turn, but not his day - a time of 27m. 55s. losing one place. Young Tony Binda had an unenviable task in his first race of this calibre - but he did well to hold his position and clock 15m. 52s. on the eighth stage.

Bill Dance stayed in 17th place. with 28m. 05s., and about the only bright speck in the sky at this point was that we were at least ahead of that renowned road relay club, Portsmouth A.C. Tony Fairclough was again fit enough only for a shortage stage, but he caught the Cardiff man to put us in 16th place , clocking 15m. 59s.

Trevor Hart remained in 16th place on the 11th lap, but he put in some good work (by the standards of the day), to return 27m. 38s., and provide Bill Curtin with something to go for on the last lap.

Bill showed his senior teammates a thing or to, passing the Medway and Bristol runners on his way to 14th place, with 15m. 40s.

items.heading: Southern Road-Relay
items.summary: Leg-by-leg report and results of the Southern Counties Road Relay at Wimbledon, won by Thames Valley, with Belgrave seventh and Dave Bedford breaking the lap record.
items.text:
Southern Road-Relay

BEDFORD STAGGERS THE CROWD - BELGRAVE STAGGER
Wimbledon, March 27, 1971

We are used to success in our own Southern Counties 51-miles Road Relay at Wimbledon - with four wins and one second in the five races held up to this year. We had expected to be pressed to win a place this year - with clubs like Reading and Hillingdon beginning to hit the high spots. But seventh was a bit below our hopes.

Sometimes in a relay of this kind it is a blow-out on one or two legs that does the damage. But this was not case here. None of our men ran outstandingly badly, but most were half a minute or so slower than they would be on top form. And that adds up to quite a lot of minutes altogether.

Our old pals of the Brighton Road, Thames Valley pulled one out of the bag to win the race in 4hrs. Olm. Ols., after pre-race favourites Reading had made most of the running, while particular congratulations, perhaps, should go to Cambridge Harriers, third, and Medway, sixth.

As usual, the race consisted of a 5½-mile lap and a 3½-mile, covered alternately.

First leg: John Bicourt took the first stage (5½-miles) for us, and set the tone for most of our men, with a modest 13th place in 24m. 55s. - our local rivals, Hercules Wimbledon heading the field in 23m. 51s.

Second leg: Colin Pearson made a sound, if unspectacular debut in this class of competition, and was unlucky in having to run on his own for most of his stage - holding 13th place with 16m. 49s., while Reading moved into the lead.

Third leg: On a better day, Lionel Mann might have done much to strengthen our position, but as it was he fell back a place in clocking 25m. 07s. Portsmouth took a turn in the lead.

Fourth leg: Bill Kerr pulled us back up to 13th, but can't have been very pleased with his time of 16m. 16s. Reading went back to the front.

Fifth leg: Gerry North was still suffering from the illness which hit him ahead of the National cross-country, but showed his usual dermination in covering his lap in 24m. 18s., our best of the day for the long stage, and can count himself unlucky to pick up only one place on balance. Gerry actually passed two men, but was himself passed by a a shatteringly on-form Dave Bedford, who took Shaftesbury from 16th to 10th with a time of 22m. 20s - cutting no less than 54s. of the lap record previously held by Bob Holt of Hercules Wimbledon (if the 23.12 by Medway's Dick Newble, who finished Bedford's stage in second place is left out of account).

Sixth leg: Bill Curtin made an impressive entry at this level of senior competition, and from this point our fortunes can be said to have been on the mend. Bill clocked our second fastest short-stage time of 15m. 55s, and moved us up to tenth.

Seventh leg: Pat O'Connor - teetering on the brink of a return to top form - picked up another place, with 24m. 45s.

Eighth leg: Tony Fairclough made our position look even more respectable, taking us up to eighth. A time of 16m. 02s is not the vintage Fairclough, but Tony clearly ran up to the limits of his fitness.

Ninth leg: Trevor Hart's 24m. 30s. was our second-fastest long-leg time - but Trevor still fell back to tenth. Such are the fortunes of war. Thames Valley took the lead.

Tenth leg: Bill Dance gave us a boost by pulling us up to seventh, with 15m. 57s., while Reading recovered the lead.

Eleventh leg: Laurie O'Hara held our seventh position, though he might have hoped for better than 24m. 58s. Thames Valley took a 12s lead over Reading.

Twelfth leg: John Thresher went off with some formidable gaps in front of him, and made a bold attempt to close some of them, and at the end was only 23s. behind Medway, and 35s. behind Hercules Wimbledon, and was closing up strongly.

Fastest laps: long (5½-miles) - D. Bedford (Shaftesbury), 22m. 20s.
short (3-miles) - G. Stevens (Reading), 15m. 12s.

items.heading: WIMBLEDON CUP for Mann
items.summary: Lionel Mann won the Wimbledon Cup 5¾-mile club road championship by one second from Laurie O'Hara, his sixth current club title, with Bert Stroud winning the handicap; full scratch and handicap results and a photo of the field.
items.text:
WIMBLEDON CUP for Mann

Double hat-trick for Lionel - Wimbledon Cup, Wimbledon, March 13, 1971

If Lionel Mann wants to go on adding to his list of Belgrave championships, he may before long have to start learning the pole-vault. (There is no club pole vault championship, of course, but it may be necessary to invent one).

Lionel started off the spring road season the way he finished the way he has been going for the best part of a year - with his sixth current club championship in the 5¾mile road run.

Just for the record, Lionel's sideboard now boasts the Lady Fell Shield (20-miles road), the Griffen Cup (5,000m. track), the Tom Carter Trophy (10,000m. track), the Blackstaffe Shield (7 miles c.c.), the Macher Shield (10 miles c.c.), and the Wimbledon Cup, not to mention the Denmark Pot (darts championship).

As in the 10-mile c.c., Lionel only just got home, however, and this time he had a margin of only 1s. to spare over Laurie O'Hara. Trevor Hart showed some improved form, in third place, while youths Bill Curtin, Peter Carton, Tony Binda and John Stow added to their growing reputations with fourth, sixth, seventh and twelfth, respectively.

The race provided a nostalgic moment for youths' coach Ron Linstead, and some others with longer memories. Ron set a record for the 5¾ course in March, 1954, when he clocked up 28m. 24s., at the age of 18. Now after 17 years comes the Linstead coached Bill Curtin to clock 28m. 00s. - also at the age of 18.

By and large, the results of the race were encouraging, after the disappointment of the National Cross-Country . Among a number of good performances was Colin Pearson's 8th place - which put him squarely in the running for the Southern Relay team. Colin only managed second place in the handicap, however - first place going to Bert Stroud, who obviously knows his way around a 10m. handicap. Good to see Pat Newell turning out again - and breaking 30m. yet once more.

The 5¾-miles championship field, still hunched after one mile. Front row: Pat O'Connor (12), Tony Fairclough (21), Peter Carton (19), Trevor Hart (23), and Lionel Mann (9). The three framed heads look like those of Chris Steer, John Thresher and Dereck Fernee.

items.text:
TRACK AND FIELD

TRACK REPORT

We come yet again to another Track Season. This year the Track Committee decided it would benefit the Club and the athletes concerned to withdraw from a couple of last years trophy meetings which were too long winded or we considered ourselves hopelessly out-classed. So compared with 1970's fixtures of seven Trophy meetings and three Southern League meetings, we have in 1971, four Trophy meetings and the three Southern League meetings. These we thought, were well within our capabilities of winning. That is providing we all get stuck in, as I'am sure you all will.

It is fortunate that, at Belgrave, we have at our disposal a reasonable quantity of middle-distance and long-distance runners. Sprints it seems we have only a handful of representatives, but what we have are very useful indeed. The steeplechase seems to be our only setback.

100m - 200m. As we have not heard how fit JIM VIVIAN is, I can only say that STEVE WHITE who is the most promising sprinter we have , will be our main runner this year - when he is not competing for Oxford. He will have fine backing from LEE SULLIVAN, MICK MARSHALL, CLIFF BROOKS and CHARLIE GILLETT.

400m One of the weak spots, although I hope I'am proved wrong. MEL FORD will be our main runner but he will have good backimg from CHARLIE GILLETT and from a very promising MARTIN BLOICE who will I'am sure surprise us all. I must not forget our vice-captain PHILIP GEE, his usual help and eagerness is a good backing for any of these runners. On the sidelines will be DAVE [illegible]EES and CLIFF BROOKS while I cannot be certain of PHILIP SMITH'S fitness at the moment, if he knuckles down to hard training he will also be a useful substitute.

800m Again it seems MEL FORD will be our main contender here, with PETER CARTON. They have numerous runners to back them up notably JOHN BOARDMAN BILL CURTIN, DOUGLAS JARDINE, JOHN KELLY, and LIONEL MANN - training for a fast finishing marathon. Also very capable substitutes will be COLIN PEARSON and JIM RIMMER (saying "wait till the track season I'll show you") another useful youngster is RICHARD LANGLEY.

1500m It seems we have no problem here with JOHN THRESHER and evergreen BILL KERR (a Vet next year by the way) our main contenders. Others aiming to get into the team will be PETER CARTON, BILL CURTIN, JOHN STOW, JOHN BICOURT, LAURIE O'HARA and JIM RIMMER, who says he's fitter than ever("I'am doing my own training this year") and also ADRIAN MAJOR.

5000m Probably the strongest event we have. With great runners such as GERRY NORTH, JOHN THRESHER and BILL KERR to pick from. Good substitutes will be TONY FAIRCLOUGH, the galloping gourmets LIONEL MANN and GUY MONNET as well as TREVOR HART, JOHN BICOURT, LAURIE O'HARA, TONY BRIEN and ADRIAN MAJOR. I think we had better watch out for BRIAN GORMAN I believe he wants to be on the same level as Bill Kerr (both are Vets next year) and is doing 100 miles a week. I hope he can prove to us he is doing the right thing.

300m Steeplechase This year I'am afraid it looks as though this will be our weakest event, with JOHN BICOURT our only sub 9-minute man. ALAN BLACK will back him up and our "Ed" might also have to be called upon. JIM RIMMER and GERRY NORTH also had a go at this event last year to help the Club out and might also consider helping us out again.

items.text:
Field Event Report

A cold day greeted our first track meeting at Battersea Park on 24th April, but what a fine start by Cliff Brooks and field events captain John Martin in the Shot Putt, both producing personal bests, over 40 feet and there is little doubt that even better performances are in store. Lee Sullivan also had a good start to the season in the Long Jump winning with 21' 7" and showing fine consistancy by clearing this exact distance on three of his attempts.

It is always difficult to keep in contact with everyone during the winter with regard to training and it is hoped that after a solid winter's training, technique work is now in progress, if not for goodness sake start NOW, as we must win the Southern League and get back to the National League. We ought to be able to do it as we were ranked tenth in the N.U.T.S. rankings for 1970 season. Just remember these dates for the League fixtures.

22nd MAY at Ilford
3rd JULY at Enfield
21st AUGUST at Wimbledon Park
18th SEPTEMBER at Crystal Palace (QUALIFYING MEETING)

These fixtures for Belgrave are the most important of the year so lets have the supreme effort and give the track and field sections the uplift it needs

Bob Cou[illegible]lault, now a "married" man, is back in the ranks this year and is at present suffering from the effects of a broken nose, although I'am assured this happened during a football match and not a domestic match! Anyway, congratulations to Bob and to his wife.

Mel Ford is in top form already judging by recent results and he has been invited to represent the Southern Counties in two forthcoming meetings in the 400m hurdles and in the 800m. Mel is now stationed at Caterham Barracks and I know he is finding duties clashing heavily with training sessions but I am convinced that Mel will produce some very fine performances in the 400m hurdles, 400m flat and 800m during the coming season. Also stationed at Caterham with Mel are Glyn Ratcliffe, Steve Inman and Keith Schofield. I hope that guard duties will not eliminate them from the League meetings.

Boxing Day Track Meeting - Battersea Park - December 26, 1970

Sixteen hardy souls gave their Christmas pud a miss (maybe) before turning out in traditional Boxing Day 2-miles handicap. Young Dave Harvey made good use of his 680 yards allowance to win fairly comfortably in 9m. 12s., a highly promising performance.

Chris Keavey took second place, off 560 yards, while Guy Monnet raced through to third place, off 220. There was a good run from Alan Black, but the fastest moving man in the field was 17-year old Peter Carton, who clocked 9m. 31s. off 120. Our old friend George Flanagan made a re-appearance in 14th place - but his allowance of only 400 yards seems to indicate a long memory on the part of the handicapper.

Philip Smith's seven yards enabled him to hold off Cliff Brooks in the 120 yards.

items.text:
BANSTEAD COACHES TROPHY MEETING - Norbiton, May 1, 1971

This meeting covers senior, youths and junior events, and we achieved a fair spread of success, if not enough to challenge for the Trophy. Although we were well behind the first two teams, we were within a short shot-putt of taking third place of the six clubs, which is another way of saying were were fifth.

Our assorted successes can be seen below, but it is worth pointing out that success cannot always be measured by position. Lee Sullivan was probably our outstanding senior competitor, but came up against some exceptionally hot competition in the 100m. and long-jump.

It was good to see Paddy Breslin back in action in the junior events, and to see John Stow back in winning form, while there was a promising junior steeplechase from Mark Clancy. In the youths' events, Dave Harvey and Simon Holmes had good middle-distance wins, and weren't afraid to try their hand at field events either. Reg Hopkins cleared 5' 6" in the youths' high jump, but that is commonplace for him these days.

Jimmy Rimmer is running with much more fire lately, and won the senior 1,500m. The senior track race providing the most excitement, however, was the 5,000m. team race.

With the National Road Relay on at Sutton Coldfield, it looked for a long time as though we were not going to find a team, but a last minute entry by Charlie Walker saved the day. With a lap to go, we were in the hunt, but couldn't quite make it, in spite of good running by Guy Monnet, Charlie, and new member Bob Ker, who looks highly promising.

items.heading: Cliff Brooks breaks Club Decathlon Record
items.summary: Cliff Brooks set a new club decathlon record of 6,016 points finishing eighth at Leicester on May 1/2, gaining an A.A.A. Grade-One standard.
items.text:
Cliff Brooks breaks Club Decathlon Record

Cliff Brooks looked good at the opening Track meeting, and at Leicester on May 1/2 he proved he was good, when he finished eighth in a decathlon competition with the new Club record score of 6,016 points. This gained Cliff an A.A.A. Grade-One standard, and a Club Honours Badge.

Our one man trophy team showed particularly good form on the first day in the 100m. (11.2s.), long-jump (22' 1"), and high-jump (1.74m./5' 8½"). The shot-putt (12.10m./39' 8¼") and 400m. (52.3s.) also produced good marks.

The second day's events in the decathlon are the ones in which Cliff perhaps has the most room for improvement - and with his basic ability, a bit of technique training in the pole-vault, discus and javelin is capable of making a radical difference to his score, as his recent improvement in the shot has indicated. His best on the Sunday was the 110m. hurdles in which he clocked 16.3s. In the discus Cliff accomplished 32.28m./105' 10¾", the pole vault 2.80m./9'2", the javelin 34.40m./112' 10¼", and the 1,500m. 4m. 53.8s.

items.heading: Surrey Championships - SURREY STEEPLECHASE TITLE FOR ALAN BLACK
items.summary: Report and Belgrave results from the Surrey Championships at Wimbledon Park on May 8/9, 1971, with titles for Alan Black (steeplechase), Cliff Brooks (decathlon, 5,913 points), Steve White (long jump), Bill Curtin, Mick Marshall, Peter Carton, Reg Hopkins, Stephen Crosbie, Dave Raffell and Dave Harvey.
items.text:
Surrey Championships

SURREY STEEPLECHASE TITLE FOR ALAN BLACK

This year's Surrey championships produced some good Belgrave performances, both from established stars like Steve White and up-and-coming men like Philip Gee.

One of the most pleasing performances, however, came from Alan Black, who has won a whole collection of second and third place medals in past 3,000m. steeplechase championships, and now ran off with the title. Well done, Alan.

Cliff Brooks looked by breaking the Club Decathlon record for the second time this season, but faded a little on the second day of the competition. He still romped away with the championship though. A third senior title came through Steve White's win in the long-jump. University studies prevented Steve defending his 200m. championship, but in the long-jump he edged out the holder, Roy Gilfrin, of Camberley, by just ¾".

Wil Wesch surrandered his 3,000m. walk title to in-form Paul Nihill, but in doing so helped his rival to a new world best performance. Bob Coates showed good form after a spell away from competition to take third place, and with Carl Lawton fourth and Dave DeBondi sixth, it was a pity there was no team race.

Trevor Hart was second in the 10,000m. in a fair time, while Philip Gee was third in the 400m., and lost second place to former champion Nick Lovatt (Mitcham) only by inches. John Bicourt had a close battle for second place in the 5,000m. with Mike Fuller (Hercules Wimbledon), and although squeezed into third position, can be said to have run well, since he had been sixth in the 1,500m. less than an hour-and-a-half before.

Mick Marshall, Philip Gee, Chris Martin and Lee Sullivan were third in the sprint relay, and it was particularly good to see Chris sporting a Belgrave vest again.

In the junior 1,500m., there was a nerve-tingling late challenge from John Stow - showing some of his old fire - before Bill Curtin added this title to the 3,000m. he had won earlier. Mick Marshall took the junior 100m., and was third in the 200m., while Peter Carton won a strongly contested 800m. in good time.

Reg Hopkins was a double winner in the youths' events, taking the pentathlon and the high-jump, while in this section, we also won the long-jump, through Stephen Crosbie, the shot-putt, through Dave Raffell, and the 800m., through fast-improving Dave Harvey. Stephen also finished third in the triple-jump, and Jim McAffee was third in the 1,500m.

The Club had only a few representatives in the boys' events, but they look a promising bunch. R. Jenkins was fourth in the 80m. hurdles, and P. Crosbie fourth in the javelin, while Ian Gillings can look forward next year to showing a sharp improvement on this year's sixth place in his 1,500m. heat, a performance which does not reflect his full talent.

The most disappointed man at the championships must have been Colin Pearson, who qualified for the 800m. final as the second of the two fastest losers - and didn't realise it. Colin turned up for the final, as a spectator.

Laurie O'Hara was again among the medals in the Middlesex championships, taking third place in the 5,000m.

items.heading: Southern League - GOOD PERFORMANCES IN SOUTHERN LEAGUE - Ilford, May 22, 1971
items.summary: Report and Belgrave results from the opening Southern League Division One fixture at Ilford, where Belgrave finished second to Enfield.
items.text:
Southern League

GOOD PERFORMANCES IN SOUTHERN LEAGUE - Ilford, May 22, 1971

Our opening fixture in this season's Southern League (Division-One) competition, was a lot brighter than the National League qualifying competition last September.

Our second place, behind the newly promoted Enfield team, put us well in the running for a place in this season's National League qualifying contest. But that apart, our lads put up a number of very good performances.

Top of the list were Steve White and Glyn Ratcliffe. Steve fairly set the cinders flying in the 200m., in which he equalled his personal best of 21.7s. to score a clear win; and he also took the long-jump. Glyn was only just under 150' in winning the discus, and gave a dramatic performance in the shot, snatching a narrow victory with his last putt.

For promising performances, however, the plum went to Peter Carton, who lowered his personal best to 1m. 53.5s. in finishing third in the 800m. Mick Marshall, with some good sprinting, and Reg Hopkins, top of the "B" high-jumpers at 5' 8".

Busiest man of the afternoon, as is often the case, was Navy man Cliff Brooks, who figured in four events, as well as the sprint relay. Together with Army man Mel Ford, Cliff gave us a double in the 400m. hurdles.

Arnold Bentt was only 1" away from first place in the high-jump, and clocked 17.1s. in the "B" high hurdles. Philip Gee showed what a force he is becoming over 400m., with a 51.5s. second place in the "B" 400m. In the "B" 800m., Jim Rimmer confirmed that he, too, is now a power to be reckoned with, clocking the same time as the winner.

Paddy Breslin made a good job of deputising for our star steeplechasers. Paddy did not have a good winter, but with a run free of injury, he could soon be under 10m. in this event. Paddy is still in the junior ranks. Lee Sullivan is just out of them, and another up and coming athlete. In the "B" long-jump, he was edged into second place by just 1½".

Derek Glendinning led the triple-jumpers, with 46' 3½" - over 18" ahead of the second man - and we hope to see him getting even closer to 50' before long.

Belgravians made a strong contribution to a comfortable victory for Lambeth in France on May 1, when, with 174 points, they finished comfortably ahead of French opposition in the form of Vincennes (106), and German in the form of Castrop Rauxel.

Steve White was Lambeth's star of the day, winning the 100m. in 10.8s. (wind assisted), and then took the long-jump, with a personal best (since improved) of 23' 4¾". To round off the day, Steve contributed a 50.3s. 400m. leg to help his side to victory in the 4x400m. relay in 3m. 25.5s.

Victory for Surrey in Inter-Counties Championship - Leicester, May 28/30

Surrey scored a surprise win in the Inter-Counties' Championship at Leicester over the Spring Bank Holiday weekend - by a clear 20 points, with 70 points to Yorkshire's and Middlesex's 50.

Contributing to Surrey's victory was Wil Wesch, who took fourth place in the 10,000m. walk on the Saturday in 45m. 02.2s., and third in the 3,000m. walk on the Monday in 12m. 33.4s.

John Bicourt was selected to run for Surrey in the steeplechase, but missed his train and the race. John was, however, brought into the 5,000m. as deputy for Bob Holt, of Hercules Wimbledon - only to finish an off-key 21st in 15m. 03s.

Lionel Mann carried Beds and Hunts colours into 16th place in the 20-miles road race in 1hr. 47m. 17s.

ALAN BLACK NEARS BEST

Alan Black wasted little time in improving on his Surrey championship winning performance. At Motspur Park on May 26, Alan took third place in the 3,000m. steeplechase in 9m. 21.8s. in helping Surrey to defeat Loughborough Colleges and London University. On this sort of form, Alan is threatening to lower his personal best of 9m. 13.2s., set up in 1967. An attack of 'flu, unfortunately, kept him out of the Southern championships. But there is still a good part of the season left for an attack on the 9-minute barrier - something which has long been within Alan's capability.

Also representing Surrey in the Motspur Park fixture was Steve White, who clocked 22.5s. for second in the 200m., and cleared 21' 6¾" for second in the long-jump. John Bicourt ran as a guest in the 1,500m., and returned 3m. 55.7s. as an unofficial third.

items.heading: WALKING - BELGRAVE OPEN '7' November 28th - Wimbledon
items.summary: Report and results of the 1970 Belgrave Open 7 miles walk at Wimbledon, won in record time by Phil Embleton of Metropolitan Walking Club from Wilf Wesch, with Belgrave winning the team race.
items.text:
WALKING

BELGRAVE OPEN '7' November 28th - Wimbledon

Our correspondent has seen some impressive performances on this severe 7 Mile course which is generally reckoned to be at least one minute long. 1970's race, the 51st in the history, was to provde a brilliant win for the young Metropolitan Walking Club Phil Embleton. The way he streaked away from our own Wilf Wesch was a wonderful sight for those who appreciate fast walking at its best. For the first lap Wilf was in close attendance and with the hills to come Belgrave supporters could be foregiven for thinking that Wilf's extra strength would prove conclusive over the second lap. But Phil had other ideas and moving down Copse Hill he unleashed a magnificent burst of speed walking which carried him nearly 200 yards clear of Wilf who was himself nearly 2 minutes ahead of Lightman. Embleton came home to win in a new record time with Wilf some 43 seconds adrift but also very impressive. Recent team performances had been disappointing for our boys but on their own course there was no mistake, Carl Lawton had a steady race but John Moullin and a much improved Barry Ingarfield were well to the fore to give Belgrave victory by 9 points from the Basildon squad. Once again Jack and Joan Goswell worked miracles with the results, thanks to Bill Ashford whose kitchen is much preferred to the public bar of the Swan as the Open '7' Administrative HQ.

January 9th 1971 - Metropolitan Police Open '7'.

The first race after Christmas is always full of upsets but for Belgrave this was a bad day. Wilf Wesch was deservedly removed from the reckoning after some 2 miles had been covered. Wilf was seeking to establish a lead at the time and in the manner of a distance runner seeking greater speed his stride tends to shorten. His strike is one of the fastest in the world so that any shortening of the stride throws him off. Less excusable was Barry Ingarfield who put paid to any chances the team may have had when he too was pulled. Carl Lawton once again excelled with a personal best which put him among the really fast boys and ahead of Commonwealth Bronze Medallist Bill Sutherland.

National 10m

March 20th - Redditch - RWA National 10 Miles Championship

In one of the closest races yet Belgrave only clinshed the team race in the closing stages when Ian Brooks of Surrey Walking Club retired with just over a mile to go. Before that there was never more than a few points in it as our boys battled for the vital points. From the start it was Nihill and Embleton with the young Essex boy really pulling out all the stops to bring the European Champion to his first defeat in an incredible run of nearly four years. Wilf Wesch, the reigning champion, was concentrating on staying safely in the race and avoiding any possible trouble he finished a comfortable fifth. Behind him Carl Lawton and Alan Callow were not quite their best but the reliable Ray Middleton kept going steadily to ensure that Belgrave retained the title. Barry Ingarfield and Dave McMullen both walked good races, prepared to shoulder the burden if necessary. Belgrave men were also prominent in the county race with Wilf and Carl featuring in Surrey's 2nd position and Alan Callow scoring for Lancashire who finished 3rd. President Alf Harley was well pleased with his first national win!

National 20 m

BACK TO THE DRAWING BOARD National 20-miles, Sheffield, June 12. 1971

As was to be expected, we made a much better showing in the national 20-mile[illegible] than we did in the 20-kilometres, but it still looked as though team manager Pat Duncan and captain Carl Lawton could do with a bit more brake horse power.

It is true that we were without Ray Middleton and Len Duquemin, who were on the Continent for the European Postmen's Championship, while Carl Lawton was not fully recovered from the stomach upset acquired on his Bucharest trip, and Alan Callow had the sort of day that everyone has from time-to-time but nobody wants in National championship. But even so, Surrey, with a score of 23, looked very strong, with four in the first 11 (individual scoring).

The race was a triumph for Paul Nihill, as well as his club? Surrey W.C. Paul clocked a world best time of 2hrs. 30m. 35s., which gives our up-and-coming youngsters something to aim at, and left him almost five minutes ahead of the second man, former Commonwealth champion Ron Wallwork (Lancs. W.C.).

Last year's winner, our very own Wil Wesch, was sixth. This may seem pretty small beer for Wil, but it represents a good performance. Our man has just taken over the management of an hotel in Bloomsbury, and he'd spent the previous night dealing with a series of crises which had left him short on sleep, which is not a good preparation for 20-miles.

Bob Coates, in a welcome return to the championship team, was only just behind Carl, while Dave DeBondi took another step forward.

items.text:
International honour for Lawton

Carl Lawton walked brilliantly in the National 20-kilometres, and clearly deserved his first selection to represent Britain in a race abroad - competing over 20-kilos in Bucharest on May 16.

But for poor Carl, it was an unhappy start on his international career. Like many a likely lad before him, he was plagued on a trip to this part of Europe by stomach trouble, and obviously it was only his guts that enabled him to finish at all. He is reported to have covered his last 5-kilometres in a nifty 44m. Although his first ten kilos took only about 51m., his time for the full distance, in 36th place, was 124m. Never mind, Carl, you may rue the trip, but don't get a mania about it.

Another Bel to have an unhappy time on a long journey was Ray Hall, who - as the reigning Stock Exchange 25 miles champion - turned out in the Stock Exchange London to Brighton, and was then forced to retire. But we still reckon Ray is good for a good 'un in the 50 kilos.

Come the Barking-Southend, our first man home was John Morris, tenth in 5hrs. 42m. 35s., with Doug Fotheringham not far behind in 12th place (5hrs. 48m. 35s.).

items.text:
April 17th - Wimbledon - Belgrave 20 Miles Walking Championship

In trying conditions Wilf Wesch dominated this race from start to finish and never looked even tired by the effort of recording an excellent 2:39:07. Carl and Ray Middleton were never far apart with Ray just failing to catch a weary Lawton up Lauriston Road. BRADFORD HOLIDAY

We usually get up a Spring Bank Holiday team for a trip to Bradford, for 50 kilometres round the Yorkshire dales. This year, we got third place, behind Sheffield and Royal Sutton Coldfield, who seem to be making quite a habit of getting home a place ahead of us these days.

items.heading: The Editor writes on walking:
items.summary: The editor reproduces the walking secretary's pre-championship comment on Belgrave's strength, then reports the National 20 km at Luton where Belgrave were an unaccustomed fifth and Surrey Walking Club took the title.
items.text:
The Editor writes on walking:

The Editor's inability to co-ordinate his contributers' contributions, so that they arrive for the same deadline, means that he is able to relieve our hard working Walking Hon. Sec. of the embarrassment of breaking the news of our performances in the National 20-kilometres and 20-miles championships.

To show our hon. sec.'s perspicacity, however, we reproduce below the following Comment, written before those two championships were held:-

COMMENT

If British walking has been through a bad patch its certainly equal to the best in the world at the present time. Each week brings a fresh crop of times which, only a year ago would have been considered impossible. Phil Embleton has broken 70 for 10 miles, 88 for 20 Kilometres and best of all the Track 10,000 Metres UK Record with a staggering sub 42 clocking. Over 20 Miles Belgrave look strong enough and our distance men can usually be relied upon but the 20 Kilometres at Luton looks to be the risk if we are to achieve an unbeaten national record this year. Fortunately some of the boys have been playing it a bit carefully and we can only hope that they have timed it right. Wilf Wesch is obviously as fit as ever, so is Carl Lawton. Alan Callow is struggling to right a back injury but Ray Middleton is on the rising fitness trail once more. Barry Ingarfield we hope can show consistently the form he has produced on occasions and with Len Duquemin back in training and eligible for the Post Office John Moullin may also reappear. Dave DeBondi and Pat Duncan are both training hard - so is Dave King. Nonetheless although we have the greatest depth and strength of any club in the world - witness those packs at Wimbledon-in the present competitive climate it is impossible to relax. If the team can just pull together on the day then all will be well but there can be no margin of error as Surrey, Met, Lancashire and Southend hover menacingly for the first chink in the claret and gold.

* - * - * - * - * - *

Now for it. In the 20-kilometres at Luton on May 8, we finished an unaccustomedly low fifth. And our "B" team didn't win, either. They were 16th. The bright spot in this race was Carl Lawton's sixth place in 97m. 21s. Ray Middleton had raced over 50 kilometres in Berlin the week before, and this may help to explain his lowly 56th position, while we obviously missed Wil Wesch, the reigning champion, who was out through injury.

We have to congratulate our old friends and rivals Surrey Walking Club on taking the title. Surrey gave us a fright in the 10-miles event, and this time just edged out Basildon

items.heading: YOUTHS & BOYS - Reg. Hopkins reports
items.summary: Reg Hopkins reports on the lively new Colt team and the re-organised junior section, naming the helpers who look after the youngsters.
items.text:
YOUTHS & BOYS

Reg. Hopkins reports

We have now in the junior section a very lively Colt team, training and racing with a spirit that would put many seniors to shame, running without inhibitions, and showing a strong loyalty to the Club and the team.

I have every hope that given the lead and encouragement from older members, teachers, and parents they have a great future and the Club will be as strong in the coming years as ever in the past, and proud of them.

Although we have had our teething troubles in the re-organisation of our section, we now seem to have settled down. Ron Linstead is looking after the older, more experienced members with Ray Beaumont and myself watching over the young and novice with the sage advice of Tom Carter to call upon, and Gordon Biscoe and Bill Couzens always ready to help, so we seem to have arrived at the set-up we desired. We also have another string to our bow with Mick Pyer who is doing a good job at Battersea with his team of youngsters.

I will not name any particular member for special mention in this issue. I'am pleased with them all, although obviously some have more wins and better times than others I can honestly say that in the things that really matter, ie. dedication, effort and perseverance, all are equal. This gives me great personal pleasure, and I feel it an honour to be in their company and be accepted as their coach. I know they are gaining a reputation amongst other Clubs for their impeccable behaviour and appreciation of their chosen sport. Long may this continue.

It is a grand sight to see them crowding round a fellow member to congratulate or console him after a race. Here we see among these very young athletes the true purpose of our sport, each sharing the triumph or disaster.

items.heading: Mitcham Young Athletes Relay
items.summary: Report of Belgrave's all-youth quartet winning the Mitcham A.C. Young Athletes' 4 x 2 miles cross-country relay at Morden Park, with Bill Curtin holding off Grenville Tuck and taking the fastest youth award.
items.text:
Mitcham Young Athletes Relay

Mitcham A.C. Young Athletes' Cross - country Relay 4 x 2 miles Mordon Park 6.2.71.

Although this event was open to runners up to the age of 20, we scored a fine win with an all youth quartet. John Stow took the first stage and handed over to Tony Binda in 4th place recording 9m 2s. Tony clocked 8m 44s to move into 2nd position. A fine effort by Peter Carton (8m 25s) took us into the lead on stage three.

On the final leg Bill Curtin took over only yards ahead of Cambridge & Coleridge A.C. Junior international Grenville Tuck. As this runner had finished in the low twenties in the Inter-Counties Senior C.C. only two weeks before, Bill's task appeared to be a formidable one. Tuck caught Bill with half a mile to go and approaching the finish ou[illegible] lad appeared to be absolutely exhausted. Urged on by our supporters, Bill found hidden reserves and pulled out a desperate sprint over the last 200 yards to bring us home first. His effort was a courageous one and will be long remembered by those present.

Running for an incomplete 'B' team Mark Clancey and Pat. Breslin did 9.16 and 9.19. respectively. Mark's effort was a fine one for it put him half way up the days overall time list, whereas just a few months previously one could confidently have expected to find him languishing in the bottom few places.

Fastest Youth award - BILL CURTIN.

items.heading: Boys Cross-country championships 27-2-71 - 2½ miles
items.summary: Report of the club boys' cross-country championship for the Jack Hampshire trophy, won by Jimmy McAffee, and the unofficial colts championship won by Ian Gillings on the same time as Andrew Martell.
items.text:
Although there was only a small field, this was one of the best boy's races for some time with very little difference in the abilities of the first four it was anyones guess who would triumph in this Club championship, and with the prospect of holding for a year that much coveted Jack Hampshire trophy to spur them on, each was out to be the first man home.

Trying to introduce tactics to his aid in his efforts to thwart the others, Reg Hopkins set off at an incredibly fast pace, his object being to open up a big gap and then try to hold them off until the finish. Simon, Dave and Jimmy were content to watch him go, feeling confident that he would soon tire and come back into sight and thinking that the main threat lay among themselves.

On reaching the Windmill they were shocked to find that Reg was not in sight; and the realization that they may have given him too much suddenly brought them to life. The Pace was now desperate, and as it happened saved the day for them. It was at the Queensmere that they caught a glimpse of his back. He was now feeling the early effort, but determined to hold his lead. The moment of truth for them all had arrived. Jimmy was leading the chase with Simon and David hanging on, on reaching the avenue the gap was closed and the race for the finish was on.

Jimmy took the lead and in spite of pressure opened a gap from Simon which he managed to hold till the end. David caught and passed Reg and thought he had him beaten for third place, but he had reckoned without the latter's finish, and lost it on the line. Final positions and times were:

The Colts race over 1¾ miles was no less exciting. With only Stephen Jay absent from the line up, all our regular colts were in attendance for the unofficial Club colts championship and trying to predict the result before the start was impossible. Any one of them was capable of winning, and we were sure all of them would give their best.

It was only the experience of Ian Gillings (it seems incredible with one so young, but Ian has been running for four years now) that brought him success from Andrew Martell. With nothing between them in ability the race was neck and neck right to the finishing tunnel. Andrew should have put in a sprint over the last few yards or so, but he failed to do so and Ian who never loses his competitive urge to win stole this race with both sharing the same time. Seven seconds behind in third place came brother Martin, holding off the challenge from new member Adrian Cook.

All runners did exceptionally well, all claimed to have thoroughly enjoyed it the only complaint they seemed to have was to claim that the race was too short!, and should have been twice as long.

items.heading: BLACKHEATH HARRIER'S WINTER TRACK MEETING, CRYSTAL PALACE, SUN. 21.3.71
items.summary: Report on Belgrave youths at Blackheath Harriers' winter track meeting at Crystal Palace, with four wins (Dave Raffell shot, Reg Hopkins high jump, Stephen Crosbie long jump, Jimmy McAffee 1000m), plus an editor's note on Martin Bloice's broken arm.
items.text:
We went to this meeting with just eight club members - and recorded four wins.

This is, I would think, the biggest of the winter meetings, with Clubs from all over the South of England (and indeed a few from the North represented) Most of those who enter are just out to get the feel of things again after the winter recess, and so the competition is none too serious. Nevertheless, some worthwhile performances were recorded, in spite of the fact it was a miserable, cold, windy day.

Our lads performed equally well, Our first win was in of all things the Youth's Shot putt, Dave Raffell reaching 11 metres with the 10lb ball. Dave is a big lad for his age, and a keen sportsman, he is now taking this event very seriously, training most nights with the use of weights. We expect him to do great things this summer, indeed I would prophesy that other things allowing - education etc.,we now have at last a future international field events man in the Club.

Our second win of the day was with Reg Hopkins doing his thing (Fosbury) high jump. Like Dave,Reg is now taking this field event seriously, working to a schedule with weights and excercises and trying to perfect a technique. He managed to equal his personal best of 1.73 (5 ft. 8 ins) in spite of the winter conditions already mentioned. This height would have won him the junior event and placed him 5th in the senior. His ambition is to clear 6 ft. this summer, while still aged 16 years.

You would think we had done well enough with two field event wins but we had forgotten Stephen Crosbie. Although he failed in the sprints, finishing last in his race, he came back with a vengance in the long jump and recorded 5-67m to win the Youths event.

Our interest in the track was equally rewarding, Jimmy McAffee showing tremendous form in coming through the field and taking a commanding lead to win the Youths 1000m in 2m49.2s. Simon Holmes made it a Belgrave one-two finishing second in 2m55.7s. We are so used to seeing Martin Bloice first past the post that we were a little disappointed to see him finish 4th in the Junior 300m in 38.0s. Martin was the first to agree on leaving the track that he sadly needed training having done virtually nothing for weeks. This run shook him up and he has since got down to work and is determined to recapture his old form.

David Harvey ran in the 600m and although not in the first four, his was a very worthwhile effort. His ambition is to break 2.00 for the 800mts this season, I have every reason to believe he will manage it if he continues the way he is going. His time in this race of 1m31.9s seems to point the way.

Our only other competitor was Tony Holmes. Although Tony is not yet in the same class as the other members he is very keen and trains hard in a business like manner. This I'am sure will bring him sooner or later up with the others. He managed, however, 3m17.5. in the Youths 1000m although still only a boy.

(Ed.'s note: Since Reg wrote this, Martin Bloice has been out of action with a broken arm. Before his accident, however, Martin showed promising form for Lambeth in Paris. The latest news is that he is on the mend , so that there is still time for some good performances this summer. As will be seen from reports elsewhere in the magazine, there have been a number of excellent results from our youths since the Blackheath meeting.)

items.heading: NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIPS - NORWICH 6th March 1971
items.summary: Report of the youths' and juniors' National cross-country championships at Norwich, where the youths were a disappointing eighth and the juniors 24th of 25 teams.
items.text:
YOUTHS

The big day our lads had spent months building up for saw us finish a dissappointing eighth. Once again only Mark Clancy (153rd) ran to form. Bill Curtin (28th) led the team home with Peter Carton four places behind. Tony Binda came 50th, John Stow 175th and Pat Breslin 197th

The whole team except Mark appeared jaded - Bill although physically below par lacked nothing in determination - to beat Peter. A pity Peter wasn't on form, if he had come 5th or 6th one imagines Bill would still have run "eyeballs out" to beat him and perhaps have come 3rd or 4th. Lets hope in years to come Bill can channel his energies into trying to carve up the rest of the field, and not just his clubmates.

Of course afterwards we had the usual 'What went wrong'? questions. The truth is that the team got fit far too early in the season and did not ease right off for the odd week or so now and again. The team manager accepts responsibility for having got the runners to their peak so early but feels that two of the runners in particular ignored advice to ease down at certain periods. The blame for our lack of success must be shared therefore.

On the basis, however that "a man who never made a mistake never made anything" the individuals concerned having learned vital lessons, and are not in the least perturbed now the event is over. There are many seasons ahead to make amands, and this will surely happen.

JUNIORS.

Twenty fourth place out of twenty five teams inspires one to write just "what else can one expect if runners train irregularly"

227 finished

1st team 64 points Belgrave Harriers 850 points
(one detects room for improvement)

items.heading: 20th March San Sebastion - International Junior C.C.
items.summary: Report on Bill Curtin finishing 27th for the Republic of Ireland in the International Junior cross-country at San Sebastian while still a youth.
items.text:
Bill Curtin, representing the Rebublic of Ireland, excelled himself to finish twenty-seventh in this event coming just below halfway up the field. The bulk of the field in this event were in the true junior category whilst Bill is still a youth. This makes his fine position even more praiseworthy. A run of this calibre in the National Youths two weeks earlier would surely have placed Bill in the first six of this event at least.

Now that Bill has been recognised by the Irish selectors, one must hope that regular international appearances over the next dozen or more years will provide the stimulus to keep him going for many seasons to come. Even if Bill does have to miss the occasional club appearance (as in the Southern this year because of selection for an invitation event in Spain) the eventual outcome will be very much for the good of the Club, as these international events will raise his standard even higher.

items.heading: LONDON SCHOOLS' CHAMPIONSHIPS - Crystal Palace, June 12, 1971
items.summary: Report on Belgravians at the London Schools' Championships, with Reg Hopkins (high jump record), Peter Carton (800m) and Mick Marshall (100m) selected for the All-England schools' championships.
items.text:
Three Belgravians will represent London in the All-England schools' championships, following some fine performances in the London championships.

Pride of place must go to Reg Hopkins, who set a record in winning the intermediate high-jump at 5' 11¾" - and must now have high hopes of clearing 6' this summer, at the age of sixteen.

Peter Carton was our other winner at this meeting, taking the senior 800m. in 1m. 55.7s., while Mick Marshall scorched his way up the 100m. track, for second place in the senior race in 11.0s., the same time at the winner's.

The above three have been selected for the All-England meeting, but Dave Harvey is still in with a chance of selection, following his third place in the intermediate 800m. in 2m. 3.2s. He only needs to record a somewhat faster time.

Fourth place in the intermediate 1,500m. went to Simon Holmes in 4m. 19s., while Dave Raffell was fourth in the intermediate shot.
